summary.text: Take \(n=716{,}993{,}899\), whose odd target is \(N=1{,}433{,}987{,}797\). Admissible exponents are bounded by \(1\le x,y\le30\), and a finite check of these pairs shows that each power sum is at least \(N\), or the residual fails to be \(5\pmod 6\), or the residual has an explicit proper divisor; thus \(a(n)=0\) although this \(n\) is not among the asserted exceptions.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
n_0=716{,}993{,}899
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
N=2n_0-1=1{,}433{,}987{,}797.
\]
We will prove that there are no positive integers \(x,y\) and no prime \(p\equiv5\pmod 6\) such that
\[
N=p+2^x+7\cdot2^y.
\]
Consequently \(a(n_0)=0\). Since \(n_0\) is neither less than \(11\) nor equal to \(13,16\), or \(992\), this disproves the asserted description of the zero set of A157225.

Suppose, toward a contradiction, that such a representation exists. Put
\[
S(x,y)=2^x+7\cdot2^y,
\qquad
p(x,y)=N-S(x,y).
\]
Because \(p(x,y)\) is a positive prime, we necessarily have \(S(x,y)<N\).

First we bound the exponents. We have
\[
2^{30}=1{,}073{,}741{,}824<N<2^{31}=2{,}147{,}483{,}648.
\]
Since \(2^x<N\), it follows that \(x\leq30\). Likewise,
\[
7\cdot2^{28}=1{,}879{,}048{,}192>N,
\]
so \(7\cdot2^y<N\) implies \(y\leq27\). Thus only finitely many exponent pairs can occur.

We can reduce these pairs further using the required congruence on \(p\). Direct division gives
\[
N\equiv1\pmod6.
\]
For every positive integer \(k\), powers of two alternate modulo \(6\):
\[
2^k\equiv
\begin{cases}
2\pmod6,&k\text{ odd},\\
4\pmod6,&k\text{ even}.
\end{cases}
\]
Also \(7\equiv1\pmod6\). Hence
\[
p(x,y)\equiv1-2^x-2^y\pmod6.
\]
There are three parity cases:

* if \(x,y\) are both even, then \(2^x+2^y\equiv4+4\equiv2\pmod6\), and hence \(p(x,y)\equiv5\pmod6\);
* if \(x,y\) are both odd, then \(2^x+2^y\equiv2+2\equiv4\pmod6\), and hence \(p(x,y)\equiv3\pmod6\);
* if exactly one of \(x,y\) is even, then \(2^x+2^y\equiv2+4\equiv0\pmod6\), and hence \(p(x,y)\equiv1\pmod6\).

Therefore the condition \(p(x,y)\equiv5\pmod6\) forces both \(x\) and \(y\) to be even. Together with the bounds above, this leaves
\[
x\in\{2,4,6,\ldots,30\},
\qquad
y\in\{2,4,6,\ldots,26\}.
\]
The corner pair \((x,y)=(30,26)\) cannot occur, since
\[
2^{30}+7\cdot2^{26}=1{,}543{,}503{,}872>N.
\]
All the other pairs in this rectangular grid satisfy the size condition; these are the remaining \(194\) cases.

For each of those \(194\) cases, the following table supplies a nontrivial divisor of
\[
p(x,y)=1{,}433{,}987{,}797-2^x-7\cdot2^y.
\]
In a row headed by \(x\), an entry \(y:d\) means
\[
d\mid 1{,}433{,}987{,}797-2^x-7\cdot2^y.
\]
The divisibilities in the table are direct integer computations (equivalently, modular exponent computations):

\[
\begin{array}{c|l}
x& y:d\\ \hline
2&2:5,\ 4:7,\ 6:5,\ 8:7,\ 10:5,\ 12:7,\ 14:5,\ 16:7,\ 18:5,\ 20:7,\ 22:5,\ 24:7,\ 26:5\\

\]

For clarity, some representative divisions from the table are
\[
\begin{aligned}
p(2,2)&=1{,}433{,}987{,}765=5\cdot286{,}797{,}553,\\
p(4,6)&=1{,}433{,}987{,}333=239\cdot5{,}999{,}947,\\
p(12,6)&=1{,}433{,}983{,}253=4219\cdot339{,}887,\\
p(16,26)&=964{,}160{,}213=10159\cdot94{,}907,\\
p(24,8)&=1{,}417{,}208{,}789=13313\cdot106{,}453,\\
p(30,24)&=242{,}805{,}461=83\cdot2{,}925{,}367.
\end{aligned}
\]
The same direct remainder-zero calculation applies to every entry in the displayed table.

It remains to note that every displayed divisor is proper. Every divisor in the table is at least \(5\), hence greater than \(1\), and the largest displayed divisor is \(13{,}313\). On the surviving grid, the largest possible value of \(S(x,y)\) is attained at \((30,24)\). Indeed, when \(x=30\), the oversized corner excludes \(y=26\), so \(y\leq24\), while if \(x\leq28\) then
\[
S(x,y)\leq2^{28}+7\cdot2^{26}=738{,}197{,}504
 <2^{30}+7\cdot2^{24}=1{,}191{,}182{,}336.
\]
Consequently every surviving candidate satisfies
\[
p(x,y)\geq N-\bigl(2^{30}+7\cdot2^{24}\bigr)
=242{,}805{,}461>13{,}313.
\]
Thus the divisor \(d\) supplied by the table always satisfies
\[
1<d<p(x,y).
\]
Since a prime has no divisor strictly between \(1\) and itself, every one of the \(194\) candidate values \(p(x,y)\) is composite.

We have now exhausted all possibilities. If either exponent were outside the established bounds, then \(2^x+7\cdot2^y\geq N\). If one exponent were odd, then the resulting difference would not be congruent to \(5\pmod6\). The only remaining even exponent pair failing the table, \((30,26)\), is also too large. For every other even pair, the table gives a proper divisor of the putative prime. Hence no admissible triple \((p,x,y)\) exists for \(N=1{,}433{,}987{,}797\), and therefore
\[
a(716{,}993{,}899)=0.
\]

Finally,
\[
716{,}993{,}899>11
\]
and this integer is plainly distinct from \(13\), \(16\), and \(992\). Thus it is an additional zero of A157225 not included in the conjectured zero set. Therefore the conjecture
\[
a(n)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad n<11\ \text{or}\ n\in\{13,16,992\}
\]
is false.
